query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation in high‐entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings is due to the synergistic effects of intrinsic lattice distortion and interfacial barriers that jointly impede dislocation climb and glide. In other words, the multilayer architecture creates periodic interfaces that locally alter stress fields and slow down atomic diffusion, increasing the activation energy for creep mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer protective coating composed of high‐entropy alloy layers deposited in a controlled, as‐fabricated state with inherent lattice distortions and a random (or weakly ordered) solid‐solution phase.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the multilayer coating to prolonged high-temperature mechanical stress (creep testing) and comparing its deformation behavior to that of a monolithic (single-layer) HEA coating with the same overall composition.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures within the operational range (where lattice diffusion is active but below melting temperature) and under controlled mechanical loading (constant stress or strain rate) in an inert or protective atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between individual high-entropy alloy layers together with inherent lattice distortions that cause local misfit strains and stress partitioning.
generation.mechanism: The layered structure acts as a barrier to dislocation motions – both glide and climb – by inducing heterogeneous stress fields and slowing atomic diffusion. The high configurational complexity increases lattice distortions, further raising the energy barrier for dislocation motion under long-term load, thus reducing creep strain accumulation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature creep conditions, the multilayer HEA coating will exhibit a lower creep strain rate and reduced overall time-dependent plastic deformation compared to a monolithic HEA coating. Additionally, microscopic analyses will show pronounced dislocation pile-ups or disruptions at layer interfaces.
generation.baseline: A single-layer (monolithic) high-entropy alloy coating of identical overall composition subjected to the same thermal and mechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold within the temperature range where diffusion processes are non-negligible (typical service temperatures for protective coatings) and for multilayer architectures with layer thicknesses and interface coherences that are optimized. Extreme conditions (e.g., temperatures approaching melting or very thick layers lacking significant interfacial effects) may alter the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of intrinsic lattice distortion versus interfacial barrier effects are not yet separately quantified, and additional factors such as phase evolution or dynamic recrystallization under prolonged loading could also influence the creep behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: (a) multilayer high-entropy alloy protective coatings with optimized layer periodicity and (b) monolithic HEA coatings of the same overall composition. Subject both sets to long-term creep testing at a series of elevated temperatures under identical mechanical loads. After testing, use digital image correlation to monitor macroscopic strain evolution and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze dislocation structures and activity at the interfaces.
measurements: Time-dependent strain (creep curves) under constant load
Activation energy for deformation inferred from temperature-variation tests
Dislocation density and morphology, especially at layer interfaces (from TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate or if dislocation barriers at the interfaces are absent (i.e., no difference is observed compared to the monolithic control), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The observed jog configurations are indicative of a dislocation climb process, and thus the stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion may be the operative creep mechanism of the present high-entropy alloy in LSR. Contrary to LSR, creep deformation in HSR exhibits abnormally high stress exponents of 8.9–14 and an average activation energy of 380 kJ mol −1 . Combined with the dislocation configurations in Figure 8 c and Figure 9 c, the same creep mechanism may also be considered rate-controlling. The unusually high stress exponents and activation energy in several traditional alloys have been frequently described using the power-law breakdown equation [ [43] , [44] , [45] , [46] ]. However, no deviation from the linear relationship on double-logarithmic curves of log ε ˙ ~ log σ were observed, and therefore, the power-law breakdown assumption may be inappropriate for the present alloy.
